newsitem.title: USA: Internet said creating confusing tax burden.
newsitem.headline: Internet said creating confusing tax burden.

text.p: The Internet is creating some confusing tax issues for electronic providers of software, video, news and other information, according to the authors of a research report released Thursday.

State tax codes which apply to electronic commerce are "often inconsistent between states and are often ambiguous within states," said Karl Frieden, who co-authored the Arthur Andersen report with Michael Porter.

Currently, about 40 states impose a sales tax on the electronic transmission; about half impose a sales tax on specific cagetories of content, such as software or cable television; and about a quarter charge a broader-based tax on numerous categories of electronic information.
Several states, including Massachusetts, New York and Florida, are studying the issue, but Porter said it will probably be a long time until a uniform tax code is applied.
Until then, companies delivering goods electronically will have to make difficult tax decisions.
"From a taxpayers point of view, they can't wait around for all this to be clarified," Frieden said. "You have to interpret it yourself even if the state won't interpret it for you."
Companies which follow the tax codes rigorously risk losing competitiveness, whereas those that are more lax risk substantial audit assessments, he said.
More than $1 billion worth of goods and services will be sold online this year, growing to more than $7 billion by the year 2000, according to market researchers at Jupiter Communications.
As technology develops, more computer users are likely to buy software titles, videos, obtain their news and trade securities over the Internet.

"With the new technologies and borderless and 'real time' transactions associated with electronic commerce, these tax compliance responsibilities will undoubtedly become even more onerous," the authors said in the report.
The tax problems arise when states impose a mid-twentieth century tax system based on tangible goods on a twenty-first century service industry, they said.

The current tax system can be easily applied when a computer user buys a software title at a retail store. But the tax system becomes muddled when that same person sitting at a computer electronically downloads the same software over the Internet from a provider in a different state or even a different country.

Many existing tax laws impose a greater charge on transactions done electronically over the Internet then those in a retail store, Porter said. While a uniform tax code may be a long way off, the states may be able to form a consensus on taxing electronic sales and tangible sales equally, Porter said.
